reason: The sources provide multi-site verified details for a compelling 45-second story about an incoming deep-space object tracked like a hazardous asteroid that turned out to be hollow space junk.
story: In late 2015, astronomers detected an object on a direct collision course with Earth. Travelling on a wild 23-day elliptical orbit stretching far past the Moon, the mystery body was tracked like an incoming asteroid. But orbital measurements revealed something bizarre: the object had an extremely low density, proving it was a hollow man-made shell rather than a rock. Designated WT1190F, the mystery debris was identified as a discarded rocket body or fuel tank from a lunar mission. Knowing precisely when and where it would impact, scientists turned the event into a dress rehearsal for future asteroid strikes. On November 13, 2015, while heavy rain blocked the view for spectators on the ground in Sri Lanka, a team of international researchers flew above the clouds in a chartered Gulfstream business jet. They successfully captured high-resolution video and spectroscopy as the forgotten space junk vanished into a spectacular daytime fireball.
angle: Astronomers tracked an incoming celestial object on a crash course with Earth like a killer asteroid, only to realize it was hollow man-made space junk—and chartered a luxury jet to watch it burn up.

claims.claim: An unknown deep-space object designated WT1190F entered Earth's atmosphere on November 13, 2015.
WT1190F was tracked by the Catalina Sky Survey.
Astronomers shared tracking data for the object through the Minor Planet Center.
WT1190F traveled along an extremely eccentric, non-circular orbit around Earth.
The object completed one wide orbit around Earth roughly every 23 days.
Density estimates showed WT1190F was far lighter than solid rock, indicating it was a hollow shell.
Scientists concluded the object was man-made space debris, such as a spent rocket stage or fuel tank.
WT1190F was a small object measuring approximately one meter (roughly three feet) in size.
The object hit the atmosphere at a velocity of approximately 11 kilometers per second (nearly 25,000 mph).
The entry produced a bright daytime fireball off the coast of Sri Lanka over the Indian Ocean.
Ground observers in Sri Lanka missed the show because rainy and cloudy weather blocked the sky.
A team of researchers observed the fireball from above the clouds inside a chartered Gulfstream 450 jet.
The airborne campaign was hosted by the International Astronomical Center and the United Arab Emirates Space Agency.
Meteor astronomer Peter Jenniskens flew on the mission to study the disintegrating object.
Airborne cameras and spectrographs successfully captured the light spectrum and breakup of the object.
Scientists used the tracking and re-entry of WT1190F as a test run to practice for future asteroid impacts.

disputed: Exact historical identity of the hardware: S1 notes it was thought to be from the 1998 Lunar Prospector mission stage, S5 notes Lunar Prospector TLI module became the leading candidate in 2016, and S3 quotes Mark Boslough suggesting it could potentially be Apollo-era hardware. Script should state it was artificial debris from a lunar mission and attribute specific spacecraft candidate as a leading hypothesis.
